snippet.textDisplay:
I don't see why we're so obsessed with humanoid robots all of a sudden. Is the idea that it will do the things humans do? Instead of trying to build a human, why not just adapt the task to robotics? That's how we've done automation this whole time. 

Even robots designed for a single domestic task often struggle with things humans do easily. Roombas aren't that popular because they'll happily eat your phone charger or spread dog poop through your living room. You think a general purpose humanoid robots will do it better? 

If it's for industry, what is the plan? Loading sheet metal into a press? Building a sheet metal loader is going to be way cheaper and more reliable. Moving boxes? A robot forklift will be faster and more reliable. 

The hype just doesn't track for me. It's just going to be a really expensive machine that's kinda bad at everything.

snippet.textDisplay:
@TheGameOfTomorrow From their website I see they use direct drive motors. These motors are great they're backdrivable, have little backlash, and have great torque control. However, using those in a robot's elbow is not very practical, because they don't have a gearbox and so they don't have much torque, which is a problem because they need to be able to move the weight of the entire hand, the wrist and the forearm. Same goes for a shoulder but no add the weight of the elbow and the upper arm. Normally people use quasi-direct drive motors with low reductions, sacrificing some dexterity for extra torque. So, they can't exactly use the same kind of motor in the arm joints.
Regardless of the type of motor, you still have to deal with the arm's balance point and its moment of inertia. Putting more weight on the distal end of the arm makes it harder to start, stop or change direction of its movement.
This is the exact treason people use cable drives.
Now, if we can get actuators for the joints with low reductions, high torque density and an appropriate form factor, then sure this could be a game changer.

snippet.textDisplay:
​​​@silvy7394same problem, the maximum locking force (torque generated by the motor) will need to be equal to the linear weight of the object being projected downwards

torque is a product of force and radius (T = FR) and the load is the product of mass and acceleration (F = ma)

so that means that we need ma = FR

for a 200N load (20,4kg, a load that human fingers are capable of bearing without damage), and assuming the radius of the motor is approx 5mm, we get

200 = F x 0.05

F = 4000N

which is a force that is genuinely impossible for a motor of that size to generate, the motor would seize and break in response to that, you would need a seperate mechanism to create a brace to the mechanism such that the limiting factor is the stress index of the material, which adds bulk, complexity, and an additional factor for wear and tear, 3 things you absolutely do not want in a prosthetic

in reality, you would have multiple of these motors bearing the load (up to 3, if you are bearing the load at your prosthetic fingertips) but that does not change that you'd need them to cumulatively produce much more torque than what is feasible

for the cable designs, they have much more mechanical advantage than these motors, they can also afford the use of larger motors, and the force they generate is linear, not rotational, like a pulley, they also afford an easier and safer locking mechanism, wear and tear is also limited as any force that exceeds the cable's maximum tension is turned into downward acceleration

snippet.textDisplay:
The scary part is that it could naturally learn to move those fingers using motion-sensing gloves — sensors that capture and represent 3D spatial movement for every possible hand and finger gesture, down to micro-movements.

That means it could literally learn every hand skill, finger by finger, directly from professionals — imagine bringing 10 or 20 chefs, 10 or 20 calligraphy artists from different languages, nurses and doctors handling equipment or supporting patients, or even skilled property maintenance workers or blue collars using their tools maintaining and managing homes and offices in professional ways.

The terrifying reality is that simply hiring these people — recording them through motion capture while performing their ordinary tasks — would already provide more than enough data to aggregate, curate, and replicate all fine-motor skills required for precise human tasks. The real danger emerges if these training sessions are extended to non-civil applications that should be strictly prohibited — legally treated like weapons of mass destruction and classified accordingly.

The only missing component is the visual cue — the point of view that enables the robot to see and then act accurately and quickly. That’s the next frontier, where machines begin to mirror us.

And that’s exactly why this should be made illegal now.
Every limb, every joint, every unit of processing power must have a hard limitation — always below human capacity — plus, of course, a mandatory universal unbypassable and unblockable kill switch!

snippet.textDisplay: The reason major robotics companies are turning to nature’s design principles is precisely why the hand you’re showing can’t truly replicate human capability. Yes, putting small motors in each joint increases dexterity, but it dramatically reduces load-bearing capacity. We’ve seen several similar attempts before, and none have matched the human hand’s unique combination of strength and agility. Also, the human hand doesn’t have 20 degrees of freedom - it has 27. So calling this a breakthrough is inaccurate. There are robotic hands with even more degrees of freedom (up to 38, as I know) and others that are significantly stronger (think industrial hooks). If you plot all designs on a 2D matrix of strength vs. dexterity, the human hand sits at the top-right corner. Only systems that fall on the diagonal connecting the origin to that corner - and beyond - are true competitors. Along that diagonal, Optimus Gen 3 currently stands out as the most capable design, of which mass production of over 5,000 units is slated for 2026 (so way ahead of this Chinese competitor). All in all, your video gives a misleading impression of the innovation level here.

snippet.textDisplay:
​@mambaASIIt doesn't scale to fine motor tech. I work in industry, everything that can be automated, is. It's not a lot, and employees are still far more versatile and low-cost in maintenance, and costs are shrinking. A robot that can do the same thing will be hundreds of times as expensive and far less versatile. And again, if a finger gets busted on a robot, you'll probably need to send it, or at least it's hand, in for repairs, which is always a premium cost over in-house repairs.

You think industry, which still largely operates using machinery and technology decades old, will rush to replace people, a renewable and stable resource, with robots, an exclusive product with copyright and proprietary parts, that will break down and remain broken until you fix or replace it?

If you as an employee, with self-regenerating hardware, with extremely adaptable intelligence and high versatility, that's widely available on the market in all sorts of models,cannot outcompete a robot, you have to be pretty incompetent.

Robotics are generally only profitable when it comes to extremely repetitive and precise tasks, tasks that would be a waste of human potential. They're also good at calculation. The degrees to which robots can outperform people at these sorts of limited scope tasks is vast, which is what makes them profitable. Machinery is expensive as shit.

When it comes to anything else, the margin by which machines outperform humans is extremely slim, when it exists at all, and that advantage completely pales when it comes to versatility.

Another advantage of employees is that they're a subscription model. If work declines, workers get fired and costs decrease. If robots run out of work, you don't get a rebate, the one-time cost is already paid and you start losing money.

snippet.textDisplay:
The thing about real life fingers is that the method to control them are all in the forearm, not the hand or fingers themselves. Fingers aren’t even really pulled by muscles themselves, but by tendons in the forearm that go through the hand and to the fingers. And these tendons are what is pulled and relaxed by muscles.

This is why bionic hands are even possible: you can use the exact same muscle control as before with sensors on your forearm. It would be more challenging to replace a hand and control it if all the muscles to control the hand were in the hand you lost.

snippet.textDisplay:
A 20 DOF hand you're calling dexterous versus a 22 DOF hand in Optimus 3 using cables. Hmm. Also, putting motors in the fingers has many downsides. I say it's perfectly rated, (as in nobody big is doing this) not underrated. Reasons why it's a bad design: Heavy fingertips = high inertia: slower, twitchier control; worse energy use.

Tight packaging: tiny motors + big gear ratios → backlash, stiffness, poor feel.

Heat trap: limited cooling cuts duty cycle under sustained grip.

Shock vulnerability: impacts go straight into motor/gearbox; shorter life.

Sealing/hygiene pain: more seams to waterproof/clean; higher IP costs.

Cable fatigue: power/signal wires flex at joints → breakage risk.

Hard to service: a failed motor means replacing the whole finger module.

Noisy & notchy: micro geartrains whine and don’t backdrive smoothly.

Lower passive safety: higher reflected inertia, less compliance on contact.

Sensor real estate clash: motors steal fingertip volume; EMI can muddy tactile sensors.

Cost & complexity spike: many small motors, encoders, drivers, thermal parts.

Design lock-in: changing speed/torque later = re-engineer every finger.

Humanoid robots are a solution looking for a problem.  There is basically no use case for them that wouldn't be better served with a a more specialized robot. As an assembly robot the "generalized" robot will never be as good a a robot designed with a specific task in mind.

snippet.textDisplay:
@MementoMori-m I just think the main difference is that Chinese development is internally worker-driven (regardless of the conditions), while development in western countries comes from the, also very inhumane, labour of the subordinated global south. China does imperialism too (to a lesser degree), but it doesn't rely on that foreign exploitation for its development, rather, it uses those dynamics to entrench its global position more or less.

Overall, I don't really care about the nationality of a scientist or engineer, and I think calling any technology "Chinese" or "American" is reductive.

snippet.textDisplay: 저는 긍정적인 면을 기대하는 편입니다. 현재 Elon Musk 가 화성정복을 위해 온갖노력을 하고 있읍니다만  생존가능성이 낮은 화성엘 어떡하든 가게 되더라도 과연 몇명의 인구가 가게 될지   지구처럼 세밀하게 분담된체제로 수많은 사람을 다 데리고 갈순 없다고 봅니다 허나 생존을 위해  인력대행울 하는 일손이 필수인데 이는 AI 와 ROBOT 일수 밖에 없읍니다. 한국정도규모의 지역을 40~50명이 괸리해내려면 AI 와 ROBOT은 막연히 두려움의 대상이 아니라 필수의 tool 일수밖에 없읍니다.  지구같지 못한 환경에서 인류가 생존에 성공할수만 있다면 인류는 더욱먼 우주여행을 기획할수 있게될거란 생각 입니다. 현재 로켙의 속도는 우주여행을 하기엔 터무니 없이 느립니다. 일론이 빛의속도에 가까운 비행속도를 달성하기 위해 연구중이라고 합니다만 지금 인류가 pilot 하는방식으로 그빠른 속도로 여행은 불가하니 AI 와 GPS 로 통제되는 비행방법으로 여행이 가능할것이라고 봅니다. 우주여행을 하기엔 인간수명이 너무도 짧은데 요즘 bio scientist 연구를 보면 인간수명연장이 가까운 미래에 성취가 될것같다는 느낌이 옵니다. 발전에 공포보단 용기를 가지고 희망을 가져보십시다.  지구가 평평하다고 믿었던시절 아메리코 펫스푸치나 컬럼버스같은 개척자들의 목슴을 건 항해 아니었으면 자원의 보고 미국 신대륙은 아직도 발견되지 못한 상태였을거란 생각 입니다.

snippet.textDisplay: ईश्वर ने मानवजाति की रचना एक गहन उद्देश्य से की: उपासना। यह व्यर्थ नहीं था, जैसा कि वह कहते हैं: "मैंने जिन्न और मनुष्यों को केवल अपनी उपासना के लिए ही सृजित किया है" [अध-धारियात: 56]। मनुष्य को मिट्टी से (आदम) सृजित किया गया, और उनकी संतान को तरल की एक बूंद से बनाया गया, ताकि वे इस सांसारिक जीवन में अपने कर्मों के माध्यम से परीक्षा और परीक्षण से गुजरें। मानवजाति ईश्वर की सबसे सम्मानित रचनाओं में से है, जिसे केवल उन्हें जानने और उनकी उपासना करने तथा उनके दिव्य मार्गदर्शन के अनुसार पृथ्वी की खेती करने के लिए सृजित किया गया है।
